1.pericope_label: By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion... How shall we sing the LORD’s song in a strange land?

schools.summary: Delitzsch calls the Greek inscription assigning the psalm to David through Jeremiah erroneous, since Jeremiah never was a Babylonian exile, and finds the date in the language instead, a thrice-repeated particle and a lengthened verb form fitting the period the contents require. Ellicott names the rivers as the country's characteristic feature, much as one speaks of the mountains of Wales; denies that the tree of the second verse can be the willow, which is not found in Babylonia, so that it must be the poplar, and suggests that identifying it may not matter, the picture being a poetical way of saying that all religious and festal song fell silent; and corrects the second verb of the third verse, which the ancient versions treated as a synonym of the first, the better explanation making it they that make us howl, so that the men whose oppression had drawn the wild eastern scream of lamentation were now asking for mirth.

Gill keeps the willow and notes that the Latin poets knew such trees on riverbanks, and identifies the rivers according to whether Babylon means the country or the city, in which case only the Euphrates is meant, called rivers for its size and its canals. Calvin offers a liturgical reason for the exiles' being at the water: synagogues were commonly built near rivers for Jews who had to wash before prayer, and having none in Babylon they resorted to such sites and served God in the open air; he adds an early father's conjecture that they were at first not suffered to live in their conquerors' cities but dispersed along the rivers.

Clarke calls the ascription of the psalm ridiculous and observes that anachronism in the psalm titles was of no importance to whoever wrote them, the Hebrew and Chaldee having no title and the Syriac giving David; reports that willows grew in such quantity on the Euphrates that a prophet called it the river of willows; reconstructs the scene at the second verse, the exiles resting after toil and meaning to spend the time religiously, taking the harps and about to sing, then so filled with distress at the thought of their own country that they unstrung them with one consent and hung them up; and calls the demand for a song as unreasonable as it was insulting, turning the reply into a set piece. Wesley says only that sitting was the mourner's usual posture, and takes the harps for instruments of every kind.

Henry takes the harder view of why the exiles were beside the water, that they were quartered there to be worked in the galleys, or placed there as the most melancholy spot: houses, if built, were not to stand in the cities, the places of concourse, but by the rivers, the places of solitude, where the exiles might mingle their tears with the streams. Spurgeon has them glad to be out of the noisy streets, sitting in little groups to make common lamentation where the water's flow seemed in sympathy with their weeping.

Augustine reads the scene as allegory. The waters of Babylon are all the things loved here that pass away: one man loves husbandry and grows rich by it, another thinks it grand to be a soldier, and each loves a stream of Babylon and not a foundation of Jerusalem. The citizens of the holy city who understand their captivity watch how men's lusts drag them about and drive them into the sea, and do not throw themselves in but sit down and weep — for those carried away, or for themselves, whose deserts have placed them there.

debates.question: What tree did they hang the harps on?

positions.view: Not the willow, which is not found in Babylonia, but the poplar — and perhaps the tree need not be identified at all, the picture being a poetical way of saying that all religious and festal song fell silent.
The willow, which grew in such quantity on the Euphrates that a prophet called it the river of willows.
The willow, growing on the banks as the Latin poets also describe.
Not pressed; what matters is that the harps stand for instruments of every kind, laid aside.

debates.question: Why were the exiles beside the rivers?

positions.view: Quartered there to be worked, or placed there as the most melancholy spot, since houses were to stand by the rivers and not in the cities.
By preference, to be out of the noisy streets, where the flow of water seemed in sympathy with their weeping.
For worship: synagogues were built near water for washing before prayer, and having no synagogues they used such sites in the open air.
The rivers are simply the country's characteristic feature, as one speaks of the mountains of Wales.
Either by their own choice, to be alone with their grief, or by their captors' order, to unload ships and maintain the banks.

outliers.note: Turns the whole scene into allegory, making the waters of Babylon every transient thing men love — husbandry, soldiering — so that the weepers are those who see the current and refuse to be carried by it.

Hears a deep sigh in the guttural sound of the opening word of the fourth verse and builds the reply into an anaphora — we in slavery, exiled, stripped of property, deprived of our worship, among heathens — concluding that God does not expect the song, man should not wish it, and it is base in an enemy to require it.

themes: By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion.
We hanged our harps upon the willows in the midst thereof.
For there they that carried us away captive required of us a song; and they that wasted us required of us mirth, saying, Sing us one of the songs of Zion.
How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a strange land?

5.pericope_label: If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning... Happy shall he be, that taketh and dasheth thy little ones against the stones

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the cunning of the fifth verse for skill on the harp, so that if the poet could so far forget Jerusalem's bondage as to strike the strings in joy, his hand should lose for ever the skill to touch them; points to one prophet as the best comment on the verse about Edom and notes that the word for rasing means to make bare; sets out the textual range at the eighth verse, where our version follows one Greek translator while two others give wasted, another robber, and the Greek and Latin wretched, holding that as pointed the word must be a passive participle though a Hebrew would speak so of a doom foreseen but not accomplished; and at the last clause glosses the children as sucklings, prefers cliff to stones, calls the practice a feature of the cruelty with which ancient war was cursed, and finds the same horror in a line of Homer. Alone among the voices he declines to defend the closing beatitude, saying that the luxury of revenge is well expressed in it and that commentators have in turn tried to disguise and to justify the passion. Delitzsch prints the last two verses without comment, the block breaking off at the quotation.

Gill takes the same line as the puritan voices on the imprecation and adds a defence of its justice: it was a just retaliation, since the Babylonians had done this to Jewish children, and what is desired is the glory of divine justice rather than private satisfaction. He also reports an allegorical reading which takes the little ones for the first motions of sin, to be crushed at their rising, and declines it, saying such a sense seems to have no place here.

Clarke reads the oath as a refusal of accommodation, since to sing on demand would renounce the land and acknowledge that the singers had made peace with bondage, and turns the two curses into a catalogue of losses — the right hand and its skill with the harp, the voice, the tongue and its faculty of speech, the ear and its discernment of sounds — calling the sentiment truly patriotic and dignified, such words being found only in the mouths of slaves whom the grace of God has made free. On the closing verses he removes the difficulty by changing the sentence's mood, holding these to be prophetic declarations of what retributive providence would bring about, with no incitement to cruelty, so that praying for the destruction of one's enemies is totally out of the question; and he identifies the man called happy as Cyrus, God's chosen agent. Wesley reduces the oath to a valuation, that Jerusalem's prosperity is worth more than all other delights.

Henry insists the closing prayer is not revenge: the exiles please themselves with the prospect of their enemies' ruin from a holy zeal for God's glory, and he states the rule plainly, that vengeance belongs to God and we may not pray for the ruin of the church's enemies even while praying for her success. On Edom he adds what the cry accomplished, that it made the Chaldean army more furious when it was already so enraged it needed no spur. Spurgeon supplies the family history: the Edomites owed friendship by kinship, but the elder never loved to serve the younger, so when Jacob's day of trouble came Esau profited by it.

debates.question: Is the closing beatitude an act of revenge?

positions.view: No: the pleasure taken in the enemy's ruin springs from holy zeal for God's glory, and vengeance is left to God, since we may not pray for the ruin of the church's enemies even while praying for her success.
No: it is a just retaliation for what was done to Jewish children, and what is desired is the glory of divine justice rather than private satisfaction.
No, because it is not a prayer at all: these are prophetic declarations of what retributive providence would bring about, so that praying for an enemy's destruction is totally out of the question.
Yes: the luxury of revenge is well expressed in the beatitude, and commentators have in turn tried to disguise and to justify the passion.
The case is left in the hands of a God of recompenses, who will deal out justice with impartiality.
No comment offered; the verses are printed and the block breaks off.

debates.question: What is lost by the oath of the fifth and sixth verses?

positions.view: Everything a singer is: the right hand and its skill with the harp, the voice, the tongue's faculty of speech, the ear's discernment of sounds.
The skill of the harper's hand specifically, forfeited if he could strike the strings in joy while Jerusalem lay in bondage.
Nothing is lost so much as a valuation stated: Jerusalem's prosperity is worth more than all other delights.
The oath is part of the resolve to keep up the affection, so that what we love we love to think of.

outliers.note: Refuses the apologetic line taken by every other voice on the last verse, naming the passion as the luxury of revenge and observing that commentators have in turn tried to disguise and to justify it; he also sets the horror beside a line of Homer.
Reports and then rejects an allegorical reading of the little ones as the first motions of sin in the heart, to be dashed at their rising, on the ground that such a sense seems to have no place here.

themes: If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning.
If I do not remember thee, let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth; if I prefer not Jerusalem above my chief joy.
Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem; who said, Rase it, rase it, even to the foundation thereof.
O daughter of Babylon, who art to be destroyed; happy shall he be, that rewardeth thee as thou hast served us.
Happy shall he be, that taketh and dasheth thy little ones against the stones.
